title: The experiment: from a prototype race to IncidentBench
intro: There are two stages. Stage 1 is a small, cheap race between the three persona methods, using nothing but the data on this site - its job is to check that the methods actually produce different predictions before anything bigger is built. Stage 2 is the real experiment: put the personas inside the IncidentBench methodology exactly as it already runs, and test whether adding personas - and which method - improves the simulation's published performance.

stage1.name: Stage 1 - The prototype race (this site's data)
stage1.what: Each persona card gets the same questions about the same actors - one per hidden later action - and is scored against what the actor actually did. If the three methods produce the same predictions, or none beats the dumb baselines, there is nothing to take to Stage 2.
stage1.arms: Three persona cards plus two baselines that must be beaten: predict nothing, and always pick the actor's most common verb.
stage1.questions: 159 questions total (CAC 99, Jensen Huang 11, MOFCOM 10, MIIT 9, Baidu 7, DeepSeek 7, SAMR 6, Huawei 5, NVIDIA 5). The agent is told the date and situation, sees its card, and answers with one verb from the actor's own action menu. It never sees the answer.
stage1.scoring: Exact verb match (strict), direction match (lenient), macro-F1. Reported per actor, per actor type, and per evidence density; every number also reported with CAC excluded, since CAC holds 99 of the 159 questions. Paired arm comparisons use McNemar's test and bootstrap intervals.
stage1.run_size: 159 questions x 4-5 arms x 4 models is roughly 2,500 to 3,200 model calls - a few dollars, one afternoon.

stage2.name: Stage 2 - Personas inside IncidentBench (the real test)
stage2.what: IncidentBench (the team's paper under review, submission 225) already runs an end-to-end simulation: given antecedent conditions, models predict the incident's status, its category across seven domains, its description, and the policy response - scored on a held-out 2026-onward golden cohort with macro-F1, paired bootstrap, and McNemar. Today it runs with no personas at all; actors appear only as metadata. Stage 2 runs that exact pipeline again with one change: the actors in the simulation are grounded in persona cards, so that responses to antecedent actions - and to each other's responses - are generated persona-based rather than by a generic model.
stage2.arms: The paper's own no-persona runs are the baseline. The new arms are the same pipeline with personas injected, one arm per method: plain record, rule card, expert read. The question is whether any persona arm beats the published no-persona numbers, and which method improves the simulation most.
how: Keep everything IncidentBench already does fixed: its datasets, its splits, its metrics, its models (the Qwen and Llama LoRA arms), its scoring scripts. The comparison only means something if the baseline is the paper's own run.

The single intervention: where the pipeline conditions on an antecedent action by an actor, prepend that actor's rendered persona card (the same JSON renderers Stage 1 uses). When one actor's response becomes another actor's input, the second actor's card conditions that step too - personas respond to antecedents and to each other.

Run all three persona arms plus the no-persona baseline over the same golden cohort. Score with the paper's own harness. Report per-outcome (status, category, description, policy): which arms improve, which hurt, and whether the Stage 1 winner stays the winner under the full simulation.

The exact wiring of persona-grounded generation into the rollout (one call per antecedent, or a persona-conditioned refinement pass over the antecedent sequence) is still being designed; both variants use the same cards and the same scoring.
stage2.why_it_matters: Stage 1 shows the persona methods differ. Stage 2 shows whether personas make the simulation itself better - which is the claim the whole persona program stands on.

previous: Both stages inherit the discipline the project's earlier results established ([GPS-Bench, arXiv 2609.03553](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03553); code: linhlt-it-ee/castbench):

One model reading an actor's whole record beat six agents each seeing a slice (0.92 versus 0.73) - single-model arms first, multi-agent wiring only where the IncidentBench rollout already requires it.

Fine-tuning on the grounded record beat every prompt-based mode on actor-level tasks (0.716 LoRA versus 0.604 prompted) - a fine-tuned persona arm is the natural extension after the three prompt arms.
Contamination dominated early results (0.577 clean-checkpoint versus 0.885 contaminated) - hence frozen clocks, pre-cutoff-only statistics, and a clean-cutoff control model.
Per-actor admission gates held up in validation (foundries 6 of 6, labs 4 of 4, governments 8 of 8; regulators 0.57) - the same gate decides which actors' personas enter Stage 2.
predictions: Stage 1, pre-registered: plain record at or above expert readings; expert readings at or above rule cards for data-rich actors; rule cards above the plain record for sparse actors. If the crossover holds, the deliverable is a rule for which card to build for which actor.

Stage 2, pre-registered: any persona arm beats the no-persona baseline on the policy-response outcome (the most actor-sensitive of the four), with the Stage 1 winner the likeliest to improve; if no persona arm helps, the honest result is that actor grounding does not transfer to the incident task - worth knowing before more is built on it.

code.reuse: Stage 1: linhlt-it-ee/castbench branch main - datasets/incident_rollout.py (OpenRouter, temperature 0, cached), datasets/score_incident_forecast.py (macro-F1, baselines, bootstrap), datasets/m5_common.py (leakage guards). Stage 2: branch iclr2027 - the IncidentBench pipeline itself, run unmodified for the baseline and with persona-card injection for the new arms.
code.new_code: Three card renderers (one per method, reading this site's JSONs), a Stage 1 question builder, a verb alias table, and the Stage 2 injection hook where the rollout conditions on an actor's action. A few hundred lines.
code.full_plan: Step-by-step details in the repo docs and in persona-comparison-experiment-plan.md; the Stage 2 wiring is specified once the rollout design is settled.

flow.text: Stage 1: the actor's record, frozen at the cutoff, rendered three ways.
Stage 1: each card answers the 159 hidden-action questions; scored beside two dumb baselines.
Stage 2: the IncidentBench pipeline runs unchanged as the no-persona baseline.
Stage 2: the same pipeline with persona cards injected wherever an actor responds to an antecedent - or to another actor.
Stage 2: scored with the paper's own harness - does persona grounding improve the simulation, and which method improves it most?
